results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The two groups, their hulls and the type-preserving isomorphism.

[F1] The actual standard-cusp theorem gives precisely invariant separated extended parabolic regions, bounded transverse limit-set strip in rank one, and compact $D\cap(C\setminus\bigcup E_p)$ for a Dirichlet domain. It includes the general parabolic case. [[thm-geometrically-finite-kleinian-groups-have-separated-standard-cusps-and-finite-dirichlet-limit-vertices]]

[F2] Properness of the torsion-free action and the elementary stabilizer computations are proved in [[lem-local-thin-components-of-torsion-free-kleinian-quotients]]. Full parabolic stabilizers are rank-one or rank-two translation lattices. A centralizer of a nontrivial parabolic is exactly its full parabolic stabilizer.

[F3] The upper-half-space metric is $Y^{-2}(|dz|^2+dY^2)$; the future unit hyperboloid is acted on linearly by the Lorentz representation of Möbius isometries. Positive combinations of future timelike vectors are future timelike, and normalizing such a combination to Lorentz norm $-1$ gives the geodesic convex combination of its summands. These follow from the explicit hyperboloid and Hermitian models in [[lem-complete-curvature-minus-one-manifolds-are-kleinian-quotients]]: two-point positive combinations trace the geodesic plane section, and induction handles a finite number.

[F4] An AC quasi-isometry of geodesic hyperbolic spaces induces an equivariant homeomorphism of sequence boundaries and bounded-distance maps have the same extension. [[lem-quasi-isometries-extend-to-boundary-homeomorphisms]]

[A1] Full choice is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].



1.1 Full parabolic stabilizers correspond under $\theta$. Indeed, each is the centralizer of any one of its nonidentity elements by [F2], and an isomorphism carries centralizers onto centralizers. Their ranks therefore agree. Use [F1] and normalize every cusp representative to infinity. The rank-one hull is in a fixed vertical strip $|\operatorname{Im}z|\le R$, because the two bounding vertical half-spaces contain the limit set and hence its convex hull. Choose a horizontal horoball $B_p=\{Y>T_p\}$ inside each standard extended region, and transport it equivariantly; these horoballs have disjoint closures after increasing the heights slightly. The complement $C^0=C\setminus\bigcup B_p$ has compact quotient. To verify the assertion beyond the compact part supplied by [F1], in a rank-one extended region outside $B_p$ the height is bounded above, bounded below by $\sqrt{S_p^2-R_p^2}>0$, and the transverse coordinate is bounded by $R_p$. Modulo the real translation generator its remaining coordinate lies in a compact interval. The rank-two assertion is the same calculation with a compact translation parallelogram. There are only finitely many cusp orbits: every cusp crosses its standard-region boundary on $C$; such points lie in the compact quotient of the truncated hull from [F1], and points from different cusp orbits have quotient distance at least the positive separation constant of those regions. A finite cover of that compact quotient by smaller balls bounds their number. Consequently the added pieces just described are a finite union of compact quotient pieces. The same holds for $C'$ and for a truncation with each $T_p$ multiplied by any fixed finite factor. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose these heights large enough for explicit cusp maps with images in the target hull. For rank one, the target limit set contains $z'_0+n\omega'$ for all integers $n$. In the vertical plane above the line $z'_0+\mathbb R\omega'$, their hyperbolic convex hull contains every point above height $|\omega'|/2$: its lower boundary consists of the semicircles over the successive intervals of length $|\omega'|$. This planar hull is contained in $C'$. For rank two, the target limit set contains a full translation lattice orbit. Let $R'$ be a covering radius of that Euclidean lattice, finite from a compact parallelogram. A Euclidean hemisphere whose open ideal disk misses the lattice has radius at most $R'$; no vertical half-space can have all lattice points on one side. The intersection of all closed hyperbolic half-spaces containing the lattice therefore contains the full horoball $Y>R'$, which is in $C'$. Apply the same argument to the source. Heights in step1.1 may thus be enlarged so that these planar or full horoball regions are available on both sides. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Construct a Lipschitz equivariant core map without a triangulation. Let $K$ be the complement in $C$ of the cusp portions $t>2$. Its quotient is compact by step1.1. Choose finitely many $x_i\in K$ such that the $\Gamma$-translates of their radius-$r/2$ balls cover $K$, for one fixed $r>0$, and choose finitely many $y_i\in C'$. Put $w_{\gamma i}(x)=\max(0,r-d(x,\gamma x_i))$ and $W(x)=\sum_{\gamma,i}w_{\gamma i}(x)$. On $K$, $W\ge r/2$. The sum is locally finite by [F2]. In the hyperboloid define $F_0(x)$ by normalizing $\sum_{\gamma,i}(w_{\gamma i}(x)/W(x))\theta(\gamma)y_i$ to Lorentz norm $-1$. It lies in $C'$ by [F3] and is equivariant because index translation permutes the summands and the target action is Lorentz-linear. It is uniformly Lipschitz on $K$ locally in its inherited metric. Here is the uniformity check: choose a compact set of representatives for $K/\Gamma$. Only finitely many orbit centers meet its closed radius-$2r$ neighborhood by properness, so only finitely many target vectors occur there. Each weight is 1-Lipschitz, $W\ge r/2$, and Lorentz normalization of a convex combination of future unit vectors is smooth with bounded derivative on this compact finite-vector simplex. The same bounds apply to all translates by equivariance. The identical formula defines $F_0$ on an invariant neighborhood of $K$ on which $W>r/4$, so also gives the needed one-sided collar estimates. Construct $G_0$ in precisely this way for the reversed data. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Normalize real axes to the rank-one generators. On its high cusp define $F_p(x+iy,Y)=(s x+z'_0,hY)$, where the nonzero real $s$ implements $\theta$ on the generators and $h=T'_p/T_p>0$. Add the needed fixed real offset to match the chosen target line origin. Define the reverse cusp map with reciprocal scale, the opposite offset and a fixed source transverse coordinate $y_0$ on a source lattice-orbit line. They are equivariant for the full stabilizers, have images in the hulls by step2.1, and preserve the height parameter $t=\log(Y/T_p)$. Their composites preserve the real coordinate and height and replace only the transverse coordinate by the fixed one; its displacement is at most $2R/Y$ after enlarging $R$ to include $|y_0|$. In rank two use the unique invertible real-linear map of the horizontal plane implementing the prescribed map of a lattice basis, its inverse, and the same reciprocal positive height scales; choose opposite offsets. These composites are the identities. In both ranks the metric in [F3] gives a finite Lipschitz bound for each map, including rank-one transverse collapse: the horizontal norm ratio is at most $\|L\|/h$ and the vertical norm ratio is one. All statements are on the appropriate high cusp portions; no global affine conjugacy is asserted for a nonconformal rank-two linear map. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Paste $F_0$ and the cusp maps. For $0\le t\le1$ choose a fixed smooth scalar cutoff $\chi(t)$ equal to zero near0 and one near1. In the hyperboloid normalize $(1-\chi(t))F_0(x)+\chi(t)F_p(x)$. For $t\le0$ use $F_0$ and for $t\ge1$ use $F_p$. Both terms are defined on the band, and the normalized combination lies in $C'$. Equivariance makes the prescription independent of the cusp lift. The quotient of the band is compact, so the distance between the two terms and their derivatives in local model coordinates is uniformly bounded there; the explicit combination and its denominator therefore have a uniform Lipschitz bound. At each seam the cutoff is constant in a neighborhood, giving agreement with the adjacent formula and the same local bound. The high cusp bound is step3.1; the core bound is step4.1. There are finitely many cusp orbits, so a single finite local Lipschitz constant works throughout $C$. Integrating along the hyperbolic segment in the convex set $C$ proves the global Lipschitz bound. This constructs $F:C\to C'$. The reversed construction gives $G:C'\to C$ with the corresponding exact high-cusp formulas. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 On every portion $t\ge1$ the two maps preserve $t$ and hence use their exact cusp formulas in succession. Step3.1 makes $GF$ and $FG$ uniformly bounded distance from the identities there. On the remaining truncated hull the displacement is continuous and invariant under the respective group, since the maps are equivariant. Its quotient is compact by step1.1, so the displacement has a finite bound there also. Take the maximum of the finitely many bounds. If $L,L'$ are the two Lipschitz constants and $D$ bounds $d(GF(x),x)$, then $d(x,y)\le2D+L'd(Fx,Fy)$, while $d(Fx,Fy)\le Ld(x,y)$. The other composite bound makes the image of $F$ coarsely dense. Thus these are the claimed quasi-isometries, not merely proper maps. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 A closed hyperbolic convex hull is a proper geodesic hyperbolic space with its inherited metric. Its ideal boundary is exactly the given limit set: for every limit point, convexity gives a ray in the hull to that point; conversely a round ideal disk disjoint from the limit set cuts off a hyperbolic half-space excluded from the hull, so no other ideal point is a ray endpoint. In the explicit model the ray and sequence boundaries have their usual sphere topology, as exponential convergence of rays in the same ideal direction and separation of rays in different directions show using the upper-half-space distance formula in [F3]. Apply [F4] to the maps of step6.1. Their boundary extensions are inverse homeomorphisms. Equivariance follows either on representing sequences or from uniqueness of the extension under bounded-distance maps. This proves the asserted limit-set homeomorphism; no estimate upgrading that homeomorphism to quasisymmetry was inferred from [F4]'s topological conclusion. [F3, F4, step 5.1, given, construct] ∎
